thread.title: Long: Revisiting the world of conspiracy theories
thread.title_full: Long: Revisiting the world of conspiracy theories

author: John Long
title: Long: Revisiting the world of conspiracy theories
text:
I thought I might pen a few lines on the subject of conspiracy theories. But I recognize that I do so at the risk of some readers deciding I’m covering up for the hidden powers that be …
The subject jumped to mind when I watched a news report not long ago on the assassination of John F. Kennedy.
As you may know, President Donald Trump made it a point to declassify many documents related to the 1963 tragedy this past spring. Actually, gigabytes of digital data had been released before.
As you can probably imagine, the assassination of an American president would lead to a massive investigation, which would collect and try to organize mountains of information, and much of it can now be accessed with a few clicks of a mouse. (Not that I’ve done so — I lack both the time and the interest).
And yet, any time a new trove is made public, the response of some seems to be “What are they still hiding???” If you are convinced that there was a massive conspiracy to murder Kennedy and are deeply invested in such an idea, no amount of new document dumps is likely to make you suddenly proclaim “Huh! I guess I was wrong!”
I had completely forgotten, but I actually have touched on the subject before in this space. In 2013, I wrote:
“With the 50th anniversary of the Kennedy assassination tomorrow, many folks have understandably had the late president on their minds. Listening to various news stories on the tragedy and the countless conspiracy theories that followed it, I’ve been thinking about someone else: William of Occam. He was the 14th century monk and philosopher who originated what came to be called Occam’s (or Ockham’s) Razor. This handy tool is usually expressed something like this: “Entities are not to be multiplied beyond necessity.
“In layman’s terms, it amounts to ‘the simplest explanation is usually the correct one.’ I know some conspiracy theorists will email to call me hopelessly naïve. But it’s easier for me to believe that a deranged man with military training could carry out the unthinkable than that a conspiracy of Cubans, Mafia dons, the CIA and/or right-wing opponents all connived to pull off the assassination. If everyone accused of being part of this conspiracy actually was, their secret meetings would have had to be held in Cowboy Stadium.”
Conspiracy theory has also been centered recently on the crimes of the late Jeffrey Epstein. Let’s say it outright: Epstein was a thoroughly despicable individual, his conviction for sex crimes brought at least some measure of justice, and his death (by suicide — sorry conspiracy fans) was no great loss to the planet.
Voluminous data has been released about the case, but as always, never enough to satiate conspiracy theorists. Where, the world wonders, is the “Epstein client list?”
Republicans are convinced there is a hidden dossier that names, among others, Bill Clinton. Democrats are convinced that Donald Trump is the most important “client” on the unseen list.
In truth, it’s pretty clear that both men knew Epstein and socialized with him in the past; but that in no way implicates either in any crimes. Epstein was rich and powerful (and thoroughly despicable). It doesn’t surprise me that he associated with other rich and powerful people.
Is there actually a “client list?” Clearly Epstein had associates who were involved in his thoroughly despicable escapades. But why does anyone assume he kept a list? Why would he? What would be the meaning of “client” in such a context?
Of one thing I’m fairly certain: if there ever really was a list, one name not on it is William of Occam. The best explanation I’ve heard is that there were names named during a court proceeding (which doesn’t constitute a “client list”); but since the records are sealed (as a routine part of the legal proceedings) no one knows what they are.
Nor, we should remember, is being mentioned during a court proceeding any evidence of criminal actions, and so people on such a list are entitled to a degree of privacy.
FDR allowed Pearl Harbor to be bombed. The CIA faked the Sept. 11th attacks. COVID and the moon landings were hoaxes. The Illuminati secretly control the world. For folks convinced of such things, no amount of contrary evidence can change their mind, because the lack of evidence is their best evidence.
